message.content: The spines of Barnaby the hedgehog were the only thing in the world that cast a shadow, and his round wire-rimmed glasses were the only thing in the world that made him look like he had somewhere to be. He sat at the edge of a stroke of raw umber, his tiny paws curled beneath him, and adjusted the glasses perched on his nose. The wire rims had been handed down through a lineage of hedgehogs no one could name, each pair of lenses ground just thick enough to turn the vast, meaningless swirl around him into something almost navigable. His quills—two hundred and seventeen of them, counted by an older self who no longer existed—stood rigid against the humid air that smelled of turpentine and wet earth. He blinked behind the lenses. The world did not blink back. There was no ground, no sky, no horizon line—only a swirling canvas of cadmium and indigo where geometry dissolved into feeling. Above and below and in every direction the paint simply *was*. A field of thick, impasto yellow stretched out before him like a meadow that had been painted by someone who had never seen a meadow but had felt the memory of sunlight in their marrow. A triangle of vermillion hung in mid-air, its edges bleeding softly into the blue behind it, and when Barnaby reached out one paw to touch it, his quill pressed into the surface and the color rippled outward like a stone dropped in a pond. There was no physics here. No gravity he could trust. No birds, no wind, no water. Only the shapes, the colors, the textures. A spiral of black ink coiled at the far end of the umber stroke. A patch of white, thick as toothpaste, sat in the corner like a thumbprint left by some invisible hand. He could not tell if the yellow was warm or cold. He could not tell if the triangle was heavy. Barnaby had walked for what felt like centuries across the impasto ridges of a single, endless brushstroke, and he had found nothing but color and geometry, no other heartbeat, no other breath. He had tried, in the beginning, to look for another. He had followed the spiral of black ink for what seemed like a thousand paces, convinced that a creature might be hiding inside the curve. He had pressed his face against the white patch and waited for a breath to fog the lens. He had slept—because he needed to sleep, his tiny body demanding it in spite of the world offering no reason for it—and in his dreams there were other hedgehogs, other small warm things, other pairs of glasses fogged by their own breath. He would wake to the umber beneath his feet and the indigo above him and the absolute, total silence of a world made of nothing but pigment and intention. Once, he had seen a shape that might have been a fox—a loose cluster of sienna and ochre that swayed on its own accord. He had run toward it. It was just a smudge. It had never moved at all. He had sat in front of it for a long time, and the glasses had fogged, and he had wiped them with his paw, and the smudge had remained a smudge. Perhaps being the only real thing was not a curse, but the single, quiet miracle that made the world mean anything at all. And so Barnaby adjusted his glasses again. He felt the faint pressure of the wire across his nose. He felt the individual quills on his back stand and settle with his breathing. He felt, in the very center of his chest, a small and stubborn rhythm that had nothing to do with color or shape or texture—a beat, a pulse, a proof. He stood. He turned toward the spiral of black ink, because it was the most *directional* thing in the world, and he followed it. Not toward anything. Not toward a destination. Just forward, through the thick and the thin, the sharp and the soft. The world swirled around him, indifferent and beautiful and utterly without him. And he walked through it anyway, a tiny warm creature in round glasses, the only thing here that had ever been *real*, and the only thing here that knew the difference.
